title: Land Deeds and Dispossession
summary: Long Island deeds record more than land sales: named Native proprietors, interpretation, reserved resources, payment obligations, and continuing challenges to colonial possession.
content:
The people and obligations inside a deed

A land deed can contain several histories at once: the purchasers’ claim, the interests of Native signers, an interpreter’s work, promised payments, and rights that remained in Native hands. Later petitions and testimony show which terms were disputed or went unfulfilled.1 2 3 4

The East Hampton, Huntington, Smithtown, and Southampton records offer concrete examples. Their agreements were written within colonial legal systems, but they also preserve Native demands and objections that complicate the idea of a single, final sale.1 2 3 4

Continuing access was written into agreements

The April 1648 East Hampton agreement retained Native hunting, fishing, shell gathering for wampum, and a share of stranded whales. Weany’s April 1662 Topping agreement conveyed only half the profits from whales cast onto the specified South Shore beach.1 4

These clauses require attention to the resource being discussed. A grant of land, permission to graze animals, and a share in a stranded whale were not necessarily identical rights. The retained terms were part of the bargain itself.1 4

An interpreter and boundary expert had to be paid

Cockenoe was named to interpret the East Hampton purchase. The August 1658 Huntington agreement separately specified his compensation for marking South Shore meadow bounds. A later receipt referred back to that work.1 2

The documents connect words on a page with people identifying trees, waterways, and familiar places on the ground. They also reveal labor that could disappear from a history focused only on the purchaser’s name.1 2

A family deed did not end every local claim

Nasseconset challenged Richard Smith’s occupation despite the earlier Wyandanch–Gardiner deed. Smith’s account records further consultation with Quashawam, compensation to Nasseconset and Catawump, and a new agreement on May 4, 1665.3

The following year’s testimony described Wyandanch’s grandmother’s residence and the interests of relatives who expected to share payment. Local possession, kinship, and compensation all mattered to the dispute.3

Native people also disputed one another’s authority

In September 1666, Shinnecock landholders protested the tract conveyed by Weany and her associates four years earlier. They asserted their own interests and offered Southampton a conditional agreement dependent on the governor’s finding and payment.4

Women, including Mandush’s daughter and widow, were among those objecting. The record does not support treating any one sachem’s signature as automatic consent from every interested Native person.4

1675: a patent was not an answer to unpaid land

Tackapousha told Governor Andros’s council that Hempstead had not paid for the Mericock lands it occupied. The town invoked its patent, conquest, and a Montaukett confirmation. The Native parties denied the Montaukett sachem’s right to give their land away and maintained their demand.5

The council asked what compensation they would accept; they requested time to consult their friends. The hearing reveals negotiations still continuing decades after the first colonial settlement.5

Residence could be made conditional

The August 1660 Montauk agreement involving Wuchikittawbut and her son illustrates a different arrangement. A counterbond allowed Montauketts to return when provision could be made for their safety, but required them to forgo the purchasers’ payments while living there. The English title claim would remain.1

Such conditions could transform a community’s relationship to its own homeland. Following the agreement into later disputes and petitions helps explain dispossession as a continuing process, alongside Native efforts to preserve land and access.1

Questions visitors ask

Open a question for a concise answer, context, and sources.

Why should colonial land deeds not be read as simple, equal real-estate sales?

Colonial deeds are evidence of negotiation and dispossession, but they were written within European legal systems and should not automatically be treated as proof of equal, fully understood sales. Translation, authority, debt, shared-use rights, and continued Native presence all require context.

A colonial deed records what colonial governments and courts were prepared to recognize, not a neutral transcript of what every participant understood. Long Island deeds were created across differences in language, political authority, land use, and ideas of possession. Some agreements reserved hunting, fishing, planting, residence, or other continuing rights; others were shaped by debt, pressure, disputed authority, or later copies. Reading a deed responsibly means asking who wrote it, who translated, whom the signers represented, what rights were retained, and how the document was later used. Deeds are therefore essential sources, but they should be read alongside Native continuity, later petitions, court disputes, archaeology, and community history.

Sources

  • Gaynell Stone, The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History (1983), pp. 53-55, 67, 308.
  • John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700, pp. 33, 245.
  • John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (2011), pp. 1, 74.
How did land dispossession continue after the first colonial deeds?

Land dispossession continued through legislative actions, forced allotments, lease violations, and judicial rulings. Key examples include the fraudulent 1859 abrogation of the Shinnecock 1703 thousand-year lease and the 1910 court ruling that declared the Montauketts legally 'extinct' to validate private land grabs.

After initial seventeenth-century deeds, land dispossession on Long Island shifted from direct purchases to sophisticated legal, legislative, and judicial maneuvers. As detailed in the '2006.2.27 FULL Whiteley Report on Shinnecock Loss of Lands' and John A. Strong's 'The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island' (2011), colonial and state authorities repeatedly violated the terms of long-term leases. A major turning point occurred in 1859, when Southampton developers and the Long Island Rail Road pushed the New York State Legislature to abrogate the 1703 Shinnecock thousand-year lease, stripping the nation of the valuable Shinnecock Hills through a petition containing forged and unrepresentative signatures. Similarly, for the Montaukett Indian Nation at Indian Fields, developer Arthur Benson purchased individual residential rights in the 1880s to break up communal landholdings. This culminated in the 1910 New York Supreme Court ruling 'Pharaoh v. Benson', which declared the Montauketts legally 'extinct' as a tribe, effectively legitimizing the theft of their remaining homelands. Indigenous communities continuously resisted these dispossessions through petitions, protest marches, and ongoing court challenges, asserting their uninterrupted sovereignty and active relationship with their ancestral territories despite severe legal and economic pressures.

Sources

  • John A. Strong, December 1685 Moriches sale and later Unkechaug petitions (2011), pp. 74, 83.
  • Allison Manfra McGovern, Disrupting the Narrative: Labor and Survivance for the Montaukett (2015), pp. 245-247.
